speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: P.E.I.-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ASSISTANCE PLAN, REJECTING CAUSEWAY AND EXPANDING FERRY SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development announced to the house last week that an agreement is to be signed on March 7 with the province of Prince
Edward Island to provide for the joint implementation of a development plan for that province. I should like today to say a few words about that agreement.
The plan itself is a major undertaking and will be recognized as such, I am sure, by the house. The first phase will require some seven years to complete and will involve federal expenditures of $125 million. The second phase will extend through the balance of a 15 year period and is expected to involve federal expenditures of $100 million. The economic and social improvements which will follow from a development program of this magnitude are of the greatest significance to Prince Edward Island and deserve the very highest priority in any scale of assistance projects.
The government should have liked to be able to assist at the same time in the construction of a causeway linking the island to the mainland, because of the obvious benefits which would accrue to the province from such a structure. As hon. members recognize, however, and as I am sure the citizens of Prince Edward Island will appreciate, there is a limitation 'to the resources of Canada and a decision therefore had to be made fixing the priorities of expenditure. Following consultation with the government of Prince Edward Island, a decision was taken by the federal government to support the development plan as being the likeliest method of offering appreciable and lasting benefit to the economy of Prince Edward Island in the foreseeable future.
I wish to add that there is a recognition by the federal government that the existing mainland links-the ferry services-are not of an acceptable standard. I am pleased to be able to say, therefore, that these services will be extensively upgraded and developed. The vessel capacity of the ferry service will this summer be twice that of last year. Modern terminal facilities offering a range of services and conveniences to the public will be in operation as well. The new standard of service will be maintained by planned additions to the ferry fleet and to the terminal facilities as traffic demands.
We have every expectation, Mr. Speaker, that this massive form of assistance will give to those Canadians living in Prince Edward

March 5, 1969
Regional Development Island a full opportunity to improve their economic and social conditions to a standard in keeping with that enjoyed by Canadians elsewhere. Programs of this sort are one example of what federalism is all about; I am sure that persons from all parts of the country are proud to be able to join in offering a helping hand to fellow Canadians who have over the years made such an important contribution to confederation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Sianfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: P.E.I.-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ASSISTANCE PLAN, REJECTING CAUSEWAY AND EXPANDING FERRY SERVICE
speechtext:
I would like to make a few comments Mr. Speaker, regarding the Prime Minister's statement. I do so with the benefit of very little solid information either with respect to the project being cancelled or with regard to the project being announced. It is clear however this is not on the scale recommended by the FRED group, which submitted a development plan. There is no way of judging from the Prime Minister's statement what the plan will be. It is clear it is not in the same order as that recommended by the study group. That should be made very clear, Mr. Speaker. We certainly want a full statement at an early date as to what this plan is. On the basis of this general statement, I must question what impact this plan, whatever it may be, will have upon the economy of Prince Edward Island. It appears to be a different plan from that recommended by the study group.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, what confidence can anyone in Prince Edward Island have that this plan will in fact be carried through, since it is being announced at the very time that the government is breaking a solemn undertaking with regard to the causeway? As far as today's announcement is concerned, Mr. Speaker, all we have is another promise. We have to know what the government's commitments are in terms of a firm agreement before making any comment on this aspect. We will be interested in knowing precisely what this agreement is.
This statement must be read carefully, because if anybody reads it quickly they may think the government of Prince Edward Island has agreed to this change. It should be carefully noted that the decision has been taken by the government of Canada following consultations of some sort with the government of the province. I would like to know whether the government of Prince Edward Island has agreed to this plan, Mr. Speaker, to abandon the causeway construction, and voluntarily accepted this alternative.

We have no indication, but I presume we will learn in due course what contribution the people of Prince Edward Island are expected to make to this program. What is Prince Edward Island's share? This clearly represents another abandonment of a commitment made by a former Prime Minister of this country. I would not want to hold the government of Canada to an undertaking regardless of circumstances, but certainly this house and the country have been given no solid information at all as to the cost of discharging this firm undertaking to build the causeway, an undertaking given to the people of Prince Edward Island. We have only been given the simple statement that it is being abandoned. No information has been placed before us which would justify the government's not fulfilling a solemn commitment given to the people of the island province.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to discuss this on the basis of any information we have, because we have been given none- although a lot of information of some sort has been leaked out from time to time, no doubt calculated to give some kind of impression. I want to say that there can be no doubt about the importance of a reliable year-round service to Prince Edward Island if the economy is to develop, and I would question very much whether any plan of the magnitude announced here will have a very substantial effect in improving the economy of Prince Edward Island, without a permanent crossing being built as well.

subsubtopic: P.E.I.-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ASSISTANCE PLAN, REJECTING CAUSEWAY AND EXPANDING FERRY SERVICE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: P.E.I.-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ASSISTANCE PLAN, REJECTING CAUSEWAY AND EXPANDING FERRY SERVICE
speechtext:
Everything I say, Mr. Speaker, is subject to any solid information that the government may eventually produce to justify the decision it has taken. It has not given that information today. It is very doubtful if the economy of Prince Edward Island can develop substantially on the basis of the plan as announced, without satisfactory transportation system.
The tourist industry cannot develop to anything like its full potential on the basis of what is announced in this statement. The Atlantic Development Board, in a study, indicated that the development of the agricultural industry on Prince Edward Island is severely handicapped by the lack of a permanent crossing. I would venture to guess, Mr. Speaker, based on experience in the province
March 5, 1969

of Nova Scotia, that what is now going to happen is that the government will spend very large sums of money trying to improve the ferry service, and involve itself in increasing deficits of an operating nature. In the end it will spend as much money on the ferries as it would have spent on the causeway, and in the meantime will have continued to give a very inadequate service.
On the basis of any information that we have now, I think that the people of Prince Edward Island are being short-changed. I think it is time the government gave the house and the country some solid information which it believes can justify this kind of short-changing of the people of the island.

subsubtopic: P.E.I.-ANNOUNCEMENT RESPECTING ASSISTANCE PLAN, REJECTING CAUSEWAY AND EXPANDING FERRY SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that members in all parts of the house will be prepared to support any development project that would assist the province of Prince Edward Island, and help it to rehabilitate its economy. But before the members of the house can assess whether or not the project announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) will be of any value whatever, we need a great deal more information than has been given to us in the Prime Minister's very brief statement today.
It is a rather sad commentary on parliament that we have to look to the press in order to get some of the particulars with respect to this project. It is unfortunate one has to look to Time magazine to find out what this project is all about; and if the information in Time magazine is inaccurate, then of course the Prime Minister and the government must accept the responsibility for not telling the house what the actual facts are.
Assuming the report in Time magazine is reasonably accurate, this looks like a one horse, one rabbit deal. The contribution which the federal government proposes to make is $125 million in the first phase covering a period of seven years, and a contribution of $100 million in the second phase covering a period of 15 years. However the report in the press indicates that the province of Prince Edward Island will be required to put up $139 million in the first seven years, and in the second phase, in the last eight years, will be required to put up $380 million. This means that the provincial government will be contributing $519 million and the federal government $225 million.

But that is not all the story. Of the federal government's $125 million contribution in the first seven years, $41.6 million represents an interest bearing loan which the province must repay. Consequently the outright payment by the federal government will be $183.4 million, a little better than an average of $8 million a year over the 22 years that this project will be in effect. Now, $183.4 million or a little better than $8 million a year is very poor compensation indeed for the causeway that was promised to the people of Prince Edward Island.

I would be interested in knowing whether the staff of the federal government which is studying federal-provincial affairs believes the province of Prince Edward Island can, over the life of this agreement, manage to meet its responsibility and also the loan which it must repay; this amounts in all to $560.6 million. That is a tremendous undertaking for a small province of a little over
100,000	people to assume, particularly when the federal government's contribution is to be a mere $183.4 million.
I think the government has a responsibility to provide an opportunity in the house, so that we can have all the information concerning what the respective commitments are, first with regard to the federal government and secondly with regard to the government of Prince Edward Island. I believe we have a right to know what guarantees and provisions are being made for the farmers who will be dispossessed under this program, for the lobster canneries that will be closed, for the industries that will be rationalized and for the number of ports that will be reduced. These are facts which we ought to have before us. I suggest to the Prime Minister that a bare statement such as we have today does not provide this house with the kind of information it requires upon which to make a proper judgment.
I urge that at an early opportunity the responsible minister, or the Prime Minister, should give the house the full details so that the matter can be debated. On the basis of the information we have at the present time I would say that the people of Prince Edward Island are getting the short end of the deal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I beg leave, seconded by Mr. Paproski, under Standing Order 26, to move the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a specific and important matter requiring urgent consideration, namely the denial of the basic right of our young citizens to be given an education in the language of their choice, in that English speaking children entering kindergarten, even here in the national capital, are being refused entry into French language classes.
Although education, as such, is a provincial responsibility, the rights of citizens are being affected and national unity is being threatened by this action. Federal jurisdiction involves citizenship as well as national unity and present policies are introducing discrimination into the Canadian society in a flagrant disregard for the principles outlined in the languages bill now before the house.

Mr. Speaker, we were informed some months ago of the intention of the federal government to hold the presidential election in west Berlin on March 5 this year, in accordance with the practice followed since 1954. speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: MEDICARE-ALLEGED LOSS LEADER BASIS OFFERED BY PRIVATE COMPANIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is no question about maintaining the criteria under the act. It is the law of the land and we will maintain that law. They have been permitted to do this because such action falls within the purview of the act. Conceivably, Ontario could adopt the same legal position.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTERS EXCHANGED BETWEEN QUEBEC AND FRANCE
REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTERS EXCHANGED BETWEEN QUEBEC AND FRANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Will the minister table copies of the letters exchanged between Jean-Guy Cardinal of Quebec and M. Debre, the foreign minister of France, as these letters have now been released by the government of Quebec?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTERS EXCHANGED BETWEEN QUEBEC AND FRANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I informed the house previously, I did not think it was appropriate for us to table letters that had been signed by the province of Quebec and the government of France. But now that they have been made public I will obtain copies and have them tabled here.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTERS EXCHANGED BETWEEN QUEBEC AND FRANCE
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the statement contained in one of the letters that the two letters would constitute an agreement between the two governments, is it still the position of the government of Canada, as stated by the minister on January 31, that this exchange of letters does not, in fact, constitute an agreement? Or is this a semantic battle?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF LETTERS EXCHANGED BETWEEN QUEBEC AND FRANCE
speechtext:
No; I entirely agree with what the hon. gentleman has said. I repeat the statement I made before. In order for such exchanges to take on international status engaging both Canada and France, the approval of the French and Canadian governments would be required. Such approval could be given either under the accord cadre, the umbrella cultural agreement of 1965, or in virtue of a separate exchange of notes between France and Canada. Since in this case there was no consultation whatsoever between the French and Canadian governments, neither of these conditions was met.
